title: Pointers to Arrays
concept: Array pointers and pointer arrays differ in meaning and operation unit just by the position of parentheses

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation: The main frame is created, preparing for array/pointer comparison.

steps.title: Declaring an integer array
steps.explanation:
`arr` stores 3 integers in contiguous memory.

We will compare two types using this array as a reference.

steps.title: Concept 1: A pointer to an array
steps.explanation:
`int (*p)[3]` is a pointer that points to "the entire array of size 3".

When doing pointer arithmetic, the movement unit is the entire array size.

steps.title: Concept 2: An array of pointers
steps.explanation:
`int *ptrArr[3]` is an array that holds 3 pointers.

Each element can independently point to a different address.

steps.title: Assigning an address to a pointer array element
steps.explanation: `ptrArr[0] = &arr[0];` connects the pointer array element to an actual address.

steps.title: Dereferencing the array pointer
steps.explanation: `*(*p + 1)` reads the second element, demonstrating array pointer access rules.

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation:
The program ends with `return 0;`.

Key point: `int (*p)[N]` and `int *p[N]` are completely different types.

quiz.question: Which correctly declares 'a pointer to an int array of size 5'?
quiz.explanation:
Without parentheses, it becomes a 'pointer array' holding 5 pointers.
To point to an entire array, wrap with parentheses like `(*p)`.

misconceptions.wrong: int *p[3] and int (*p)[3] are the same.
misconceptions.correct: The former is an 'array of pointers'; the latter is a 'pointer to an array'.
misconceptions.why: Due to operator precedence, `[]` binds before `*`, so parentheses completely change the meaning.

keyTakeaway: When you want to point to an entire array as one unit, use an array pointer: `TYPE (*NAME)[SIZE]`.
